title: Four sons from the fire
hookLine: a demon king who scorned humans, and why God comes down as one
carry: avatar: God comes down as one of us

cards: While the priests on earth pour offerings into Dasharatha's fire, the gods hold a meeting of their own. They go to Brahma with a complaint.
Ravana, king of the rakshasas, is tormenting all the worlds, and nobody can stop him. Why not? Because Brahma himself gave him a boon.
Ravana asked never to be killed by gods, or demons, or celestial beings of any kind. He listed nearly everyone, and left out one group, because he thought them too weak to bother with.

teach.b: Ravana left out human beings. He scorned them. So Brahma says: he can be killed by a human.
And Vishnu agrees to be born as a man, in four parts, as the four sons of Dasharatha. Down on earth, Rishyashringa begins a second rite, for the sake of sons.

teach.h: A VESSEL OF PAYASA FROM THE FIRE.
teach.b: Out of the fire rises a great shining being, carrying a golden vessel. Inside is payasa, sweet rice cooked in milk, made by the gods. Give this to your queens, he tells Dasharatha.

The king divides it: half to Kausalya, and the rest shared between Sumitra and Kaikeyi, Sumitra receiving two shares. In time, four sons are born. Rama to Kausalya, on the ninth day of the bright half of Chaitra.
Bharata to Kaikeyi. And to Sumitra, twins: Lakshmana and Shatrughna. The loophole is the whole point.
Ravana thought humans didn't count, and God came as one.
Hindus call this avatar, literally a descent: Vishnu coming down into the world in the form it needs.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whenever dharma declines, he comes, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma right.
So Rama Navami isn't only a birthday.
Hindus keep it with fasting, readings of the Ramayana, and in some temples a cradle for the infant Rama: God, small enough to rock. Now the week, from the top. The whole story in chapter one.
The poet from the anthill. Two birds, and grief becoming verse. Brahma's promise.
A king at the sacred fire. A guest who brought the rain. And today, four boys, and God come down as one of us.

how: Hindus celebrate Rama Navami, Rama's birthday, on the ninth day of the bright half of Chaitra, with fasting, temple worship, readings of the Ramayana, and in some places a cradle for the infant Rama.

o: the rite whose fruit is payasa and four sons
a gift Ravana demands from every king he defeats
the rite where Vishnu first battles Ravana

games.q: who was born to whom — tap the pairs.
p: sweet rice in milk, from the fire

s: Ravana's boon protected him from human beings
he left humans out because he scorned them. that's the loophole.
avatar means God coming down into the world
Vishnu descends as Rama, a human, to set dharma right.
Rama Navami falls in the month of Chaitra
the ninth day of the bright half, Rama's birthday.

games.q: you're the gods. Ravana can't be killed by any god or demon. what do you do?
o: make Ravana a stronger enemy among the gods.
send someone as a human being.
wait for Ravana to grow old.
games.why: Ravana scorned humans and never asked protection from them. Vishnu agrees to be born as a man, as Dasharatha's four sons: an avatar, God coming down.

practice: Many Hindus chant a short mantra to Rama: Shri Rama, Jaya Rama, Jaya Jaya Rama. If you pray, say it softly with the breath.
If you don't, bring to mind one ordinary person, the kind Ravana would have overlooked, and breathe as if they matter. In this story, the one nobody counted is where God turned up.

wordCard.voice: Dasharatha's sacrifice. Its fruit is the payasa from the fire, shared among three queens, and four sons, born to undo Ravana's boast.

orig.note: Sanskrit pāyasa: rice cooked in milk, a sweet pudding. still made for festivals as payasam or kheer.

carryVoice: Your line: avatar, God comes down as one of us. Ravana never counted on a human. A week, done.
